additions.reason: The source text twice uses the phrase 'לְמַעְלָה לְמַעְלָה עַד אֵין סוֹף' as the explicit structural endpoint of the yirah chain. The infinite ascent is the Torah's central metaphysical claim: fear contains fear to infinity. אֵין סוֹף here is not the Kabbalistic technical term for Godhead per se, but the qualitative descriptor of the infinite height of יִרְאָה — the teaching declares that יִרְאָה reaches up to אֵין סוֹף (the unlimited). A bechina edge יראה ↔ אין סוף — expressing that the nature of yirah is infinite — should be added. The bechina language is 'וְכֵן נִכְלָל יִרְאָה אַחַת בַּחֲבֶרְתָּהּ, לְמַעְלָה לְמַעְלָה עַד אֵין סוֹף', identifying the infinite recursive quality as the essential nature of יִרְאָה.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: The word עָקֵב appears in the verse 'עֵקֶב עֲנָוָה יִרְאַת ה'' and is translated by the Rebbe as meaning 'outcome/heel of humility'. However, עָקֵב here is a grammatical connector in the verse, not a concept the Rebbe establishes as having its own bechina. The Rebbe says 'עֲקֵב הָעֲנָוָה הִיא יִרְאָה' — the heel-of-humility IS fear — using עָקֵב as a construct noun (smikhut). The bechina runs between עֲנָוָה and יִרְאָה, not עָקֵב as an independent concept. Excluded from the package.

The Midrash says 'עָשְׂתָה חָכְמָה עֲטָרָה עַל רֹאשָׁהּ' — wisdom made [fear] a crown on its head. The Rebbe cites this as part of the proof that fear reaches to infinity (fear serves as both a crown AND a heel, at different levels). However, עֲטָרָה is not declared a bechina of יִרְאָה by the Rebbe — it is the Midrash's description of the relationship between חָכְמָה and יִרְאָה (i.e., fear is the crown that wisdom wears). This is more of a metaphor for their structural relationship than an independent bechina-node. The bechina structure is חָכְמָה ↔ יִרְאָה; עֲטָרָה is the descriptive metaphor for how they relate. Not added as a separate node.

The Midrash says 'עָשְׂתָה עֲנָוָה עָקֵב לְסִלּוּתָא' — humility made fear a heel for a footstool. סִלּוּתָא (Aramaic: something despised/stepped on) describes how humility appears to treat fear as its lowest rung. This is the contrast term in the Midrash's rhetoric (footstool vs. crown), not a bechina-concept the Rebbe equates with anything. It is descriptive context, not a bechina node. Excluded.

The phrase 'מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה' is the subject of the opening sentence — it is the same as יִרְאָה, used as a formal noun (the attribute/quality of fear). The Rebbe says 'מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה בְּעַצְמָהּ הִיא יְרֵאָה' — the very attribute of fear is itself afraid. This is the self-referential claim: יִרְאָה = מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה. Rather than a separate bechina node, מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה is a circumlocution for יִרְאָה itself. It would be an alias/variant of יִרְאָה, not a distinct concept. The bechina edge here is יִרְאָה ↔ יִרְאָה (reflexive — the attribute IS afraid), which is better expressed structurally as the self-recursive property of the node יִרְאָה. Not added as a separate concept node.

The phrase 'יֵשׁ יִרְאָה לְמַעְלָה מִיִּרְאָה' describes the infinite regress structure — it is a conclusion statement, not a named bechina concept. The concept is captured by the יִרְאָה ↔ אֵין סוֹף edge. Not a separate node.

analysis_notes.note_on_evil_mirror: Torah #148 contains no evil counterpart, negative domain, or opposing concept cluster. The teaching is a pure philosophical observation about the infinite recursive nature of יִרְאָה — the 'good' pole only. The Midrash contrasted humility (making fear a footstool) with wisdom (making fear a crown), but both represent positive virtues and the contrast is not a good/evil polarity. No evil-mirror gap analysis is needed.
